claims.text: The proposed framework applies to Fe-Co-Ni-based fcc high-entropy alloys, exemplified by equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The relevant state is paramagnetic over approximately 50–1200 K and Wigner-Seitz radii of about 2.62–2.68 Bohr.
Static calculations predict zero or small magnetic moments for Co, Cr, and Ni in this system.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations thermally induce sizable magnetic moments on Co, Cr, and Ni.
In the LSF calculation, magnetic entropy is evaluated from thermally averaged magnetic moments rather than static equilibrium moments.
LSF-induced moments alter magnetic entropy and internal-energy contributions to the free energy.
Magnetic free-energy changes, together with magneto-volume effects, modify the stacking-fault energy.
Including LSFs gives a lower stacking-fault-energy magnitude than floating-spin calculations.
A lower stacking-fault energy under LSF modeling increases the predicted propensity for stacking faults and nano-twins relative to static modeling.
Increasing temperature raises the stacking-fault energy through magneto-volume coupling and suppresses stacking faults and nano-twins.
Including LSFs shifts the temperature of the transition from twinning-induced plasticity to slip-dominated deformation.
Static mean-field approaches significantly underestimate the orbital-moment contribution to magnetic entropy.
The orbital-moment contribution is a critical previously neglected factor in the free-energy landscape controlling stacking-fault and deformation behavior.
Conventional floating-spin calculations use static equilibrium moments and do not capture thermal longitudinal spin fluctuations.
Floating-spin calculations predict higher stacking-fault-energy magnitudes than LSF calculations.
Static or floating-spin approaches underestimate magnetic entropy relative to the LSF treatment.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to paramagnetic states in which thermal spin fluctuations are significant.
Explicit phonon effects are not included in the cited LSF theory and their omission may affect quantitative agreement with experimental stacking-fault energies.
The cited results are simulated and rely on the fluctuating-medium approximation and a one-shot static-equilibrium approach.
The cited evidence does not explicitly quantify an orbital-moment contribution; the hypothesis infers it from a magnetic-entropy expression based on magnetic moments.
